turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: So you're here about your sleep. How many hours are you getting a night?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Maybe five? It depends on the night.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: Do you drink coffee after lunch?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Usually one around three, yeah.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: And do you look at your phone in bed?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Sometimes. It helps me wind down.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: Well, it doesn't. The blue light keeps your brain awake. You need to stop using your phone at night.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I've heard that. It's just the only time I get to myself.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: Your phone time is the only time that's yours.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Pretty much. Once the kids are down, that hour is mine.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: That hour is something you protect because nothing else in the day belongs to you. Are you exercising at all?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Not really. I'm too tired.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: Have you tried melatonin? Just take three milligrams before bed, that's what most people do.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I don't really like taking pills.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: It's a supplement, not really a medication, so it's pretty mild.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Maybe. I don't know.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: Okay. So less phone, no coffee after noon, and try the melatonin. Does that sound good?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I guess I could try the coffee thing.

turns.speaker: practitioner
turns.text: Cutting the afternoon coffee is something you could try. Anything else?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: No, I think that's it.
